passages.quote: Subcritical multiplication is the effect of fissions in the fuel increasing the effective source strength of a reactor with a keff less than one.
Subcritical multiplication factor is the factor that relates the source level to the steady-state neutron level of the core.
A neutron source strength of 100 neutrons per generation will result in 250 neutrons per generation being produced from a combination of sources and fission in a shutdown reactor with a keff of 0.6.
Notice from this example that the count rate doubled as the reactivity was halved (e.g., reactivity was changed from -1000 pcm to -500 pcm).
For a critical reactor, 1/M is equal to zero.
1/M plots can be used to predict the point of criticality.

The neutron population will typically reach its new steady-state value within 1-2 minutes, but the closer the reactor is to criticality, the longer the time will be to stabilize the neutron population.
Reactor period is the time required for reactor power to change by a factor of e (2.718).
Doubling time is the time required for reactor power to double.
Reactor startup rate is the number of factors of ten that reactor power changes in one minute.
If the reactor period is positive, reactor power is increasing.
is the weighted average of the total delayed neutron fractions of the different types of fuel used in a particular reactor.
delayed neutrons are born at lower average energies than fast neutrons.
Prompt jump is the small, immediate power increase that follows a positive reactivity insertion related to an increase in the prompt neutron population.
Prompt drop is the small, immediate power decrease that follows a negative reactivity insertion related to a decrease in the prompt neutron population.
Prompt critical is the condition when the reactor is critical on prompt neutrons alone.
When a reactor is prompt critical, the neutron population, and hence power, can increase as quickly as the prompt neutron generation time allows.
A reactor whose reactivity even approaches prompt critical is likely to suffer damage due to the rapid rise in power to a very high level.
Measuring reactivity in units of dollars is useful when determining if a reactor is prompt critical.
A reactivity unit related to the dollar is the cent, where one cent is one-hundredth of a dollar.
Because the effective delayed neutron fraction is dependent upon the nuclides used as fuel, the value of the dollar is also dependent on the nuclides used as fuel.

An installed neutron source, together with the subcritical multiplication process, may be needed to increase the neutron population to a level where it can be monitored throughout the startup procedure.

Without the installed source, it may be possible to withdraw the control rods to the point of criticality, and then continue withdrawal without detecting criticality because the reactor goes critical below the indicating range.
An alternative to using a startup source is to limit the rate of rod withdrawal, or require waiting periods between rod withdrawal increments.
A reactivity balance called an Estimated Critical Position is used to predict the position of the control rods at which criticality will be achieved during a startup.
This process provides an added margin of safety because a large discrepancy between actual and estimated critical rod positions would indicate that the core was not performing as designed.
In fast reactor systems, reflectors are not composed of moderating materials because it is desired to keep neutron energy high.
The reflector functions by scattering some of the neutrons, which would have leaked from a bare (unreflected) core, back into the fuel to produce additional fissions.
Varying fuel concentrations or poison loading for flux shaping is frequently referred to as zoning.
Power tilt is a non-symmetrical variation of core power in one quadrant of the core relative to the other quadrants.

Shutdown margin is the instantaneous amount of reactivity by which a reactor is subcritical or would be subcritical from its present condition assuming all control rods are fully inserted except for the single rod with the highest integral worth, which is assumed to be fully withdrawn.
The stuck rod criterion is applied to the shutdown margin to ensure that the failure of a single control rod will not prevent the control rod system from shutting down the reactor.
Shutdown margin is required to exist at all times, even when the reactor is critical.
The inherent stability and power turning ability of a negative temperature coefficient are ineffective below the point of adding heat.
The half-life of the longest lived delayed neutron precursor results in a reactor period of around -80 seconds or a startup rate of -1/3 DPM for most reactors after a reactor shutdown.
Decay heat is always present following reactor operation due to energy resulting from the decay of fission products.
The amount of decay heat production after shutdown is directly influenced by the power history of the reactor prior to shutdown.
This decay heat generation rate diminishes to less than 1% approximately one hour after shutdown.
Decay heat is a long-term consideration and impacts spent fuel handling, reprocessing, waste management, and reactor safety.
It is the factor by which source neutrons are multiplied to get neutron population

body.text: β is the fraction of all fission neutrons born delayed for a particular type of fuel.
The effective fraction is the average fraction multiplied by an importance factor, which accounts for the fact that
Delayed neutrons average about 0.5 MeV, compared with about 2 MeV for prompt neutrons.
τ = ℓ*/ρ + (β̄eff - ρ) / (λeff ρ + ρ̇)   (prompt term plus delayed term)

τ is reactor period, ℓ* is prompt generation lifetime, β̄eff is the effective delayed neutron fraction, ρ is reactivity, λeff is the effective precursor decay constant, and ρ̇ is the rate of change of reactivity.
Stable period: τ = (β̄eff - ρ) / (λeff ρ)
Approximate values for λeff are 0.08 per second at steady state, 0.1 per second for a power increase, and 0.05 per second for a power decrease.

summary.text: A subcritical reactor multiplies its source by M = 1 / (1 - keff). 1/M plots predict criticality.
Period, doubling time and startup rate describe power change.
Prompt jump and prompt drop are small, immediate changes. One dollar of reactivity is prompt critical.
Fast reactor reflectors are not moderating materials.
Shutdown margin assumes the highest worth rod is fully withdrawn.
Decay heat comes from fission product decay and falls to less than 1% about one hour after shutdown.

blend_notes.note: The handbook p.33 and p.34 say decay heat right after shutdown is about 5 to 6%. The Batch 5 decision says the handbook's 7%, taken from the HT material, and hides 6%. The two handbook statements differ, so neither starting value is on this page. NP-01 p.62's seven percent is a share of fission energy. Existing Q56 says 5-6%.

Delayed neutron totals differ inside the handbook: NP-04 Table 1 gives U-238 0.0157 and Pu-239 0.00200, p.31 gives U-235 0.0064, and NP-02 p.30 gives 0.0148, 0.0021 and 0.0065. The page gives no fractions and sends the learner to NP-02.
